**Now, bigger design review — anything functionally wrong?**

1. **Nut corner chamfer vs snap ring:** Real hex nuts have chamfered corners (the top/bottom faces are chamfered so the "corner" diameter is reduced near the faces). The ring at 1.0–1.9 mm above the nut bottom engages the full-flat zone. ✓

So as layers go up: at z=10.9 the pocket suddenly NARROWS from af1 to af2 — meaning material appears in the ring annulus (between af2 and af1 hexes) with nothing directly beneath it except... wait no. Let me think again.

The pocket at z 9.9–10.9 is af1 hex (wide). The pocket at z 10.9–11.8 is af2 hex (narrow). So the solid at z 10.9–11.8 = full disc minus af2 hex = disc with narrow hex hole. The solid at z 9.9–10.9 = disc minus af1 hex = disc with wide hex hole. When printing, at z=10.9 we start printing the ring annulus (material between af2 hex and af1 hex boundary). Directly below that annulus is the af1 hex hole — i.e., the ring's underside is unsupported over the gap between af2 hex edge and af1 hex edge: width (af1−af2)/2 = 0.175 mm. A 0.175 mm bridge — trivially printable, the first ring layer will fuse to the walls on both sides... wait, no! The ring annulus underside spans from the af2 hex wall (inner) to the af1 hex wall (outer) — but the af1 hex wall below is the pocket wall; the ring annulus sits INSIDE the pocket void below. The "bridge" is between the ring's inner edge (af2 wall) and outer edge (af1 wall)? No wait — at z just below 10.9, the pocket hole is af1 hex. The ring annulus at z ≥ 10.9 occupies the region between af2 hex and af1 hex. Its underside (z=10.9 plane) is entirely over the af1 hex hole → unsupported except at... nothing. It's an annular bridge of width (af1−af2)/2 = 0.175 mm... no wait, the annulus width: af1 hex minus af2 hex region. The annulus is bounded inside by af2 hex, outside by af1 hex. Radial width = (af1−af2)/2 = 0.175 mm at flats; at corners: (d1−d2)/2 = (9.353−8.949)/2 = 0.202 mm. So the ring underside is a 0.175–0.2 mm wide annular bridge loop, ~29 mm perimeter. Printing a 0.2 mm wide ring overhang: the first layer of it will sag slightly into the hole but since it's only 0.2 mm wide, the extrusion (0.42 mm wide line) will actually rest on... hmm, actually a 0.2 mm annular gap can't even fit one 0.42 mm extrusion line properly. The slicer will treat the region between af2 and af1 hexes at z≥10.9 as solid; at z<10.9 that region is empty. When printing the first ring layer, the extrusion line (0.42 mm wide) will be centered on the 0.2 mm annulus and will mostly fuse with the adjacent walls... Actually the walls ARE adjacent: the inner boundary of the annulus is the af2 pocket wall — but that wall at z<10.9 doesn't exist (pocket is wider below). Hmm, no: the pocket wall below the ring is the af1 hex wall, which is 0.175 mm radially OUTSIDE the ring's outer edge. So the ring's first layer: a 0.2 mm annulus with open space on BOTH sides (inside: af2 hole continues up; outside: af1 hole continues down). It's a freestanding 0.2 mm wide annulus — bridging a "ring" 0.2 mm wide. That's a classic small bridging case; slicers handle it as bridges; PLA bridges fine. The bridge is only 0.2 mm wide but 29 mm long path — it's a bridge segment of width 0.2 and length... the bridge direction: the extrusion runs around the annulus; each little segment is supported at both ends by... hmm, what supports the ring layer at its start/end? The annulus is a closed loop — a closed loop bridge has no ends! A closed-loop bridge of 0.2 mm width: the slicer prints it as a closed loop; each point of the loop is supported only by tension... closed loop bridges actually work OK because the loop is continuous — no free ends to sag. Actually closed loops bridge better than open spans? A closed circular bridge will sag as a whole (it has no anchor at all!). Wait — is that right? The ring at z 10.9–11.8: its underside at z=10.9 is over the af1 hole. But hold on — is the OUTER edge of the ring connected to anything below? The af1 pocket wall at z 9.9–10.9 — the solid is OUTSIDE the af1 hex. The ring's outer edge is exactly AT the af1 hex boundary. So the ring's outer edge is directly above the pocket wall top edge — the ring touches solid material along its outer edge! The af1 wall below supports the ring's outer 0 mm... the outer edge line of the ring is coincident with the top edge of the af1 wall below. So the ring layer at z=10.9 is connected to the wall below along its outer boundary line (tangent contact — zero-width support, but in practice the extrusion is 0.42 wide and the wall below is right there, so the outer half of the ring extrusion fuses to the wall top). Hmm, wait, that's wrong too: the pocket wall below (af1 hex at z 9.9–10.9) — its top face at z=10.9 IS the plane where the ring annulus begins... 

Ugh, let me re-set this. Solid regions:
- z ∈ [9.9, 10.9]: solid = disc − af1 hex. The af1 hex wall is vertical here; the pocket void is af1 hex.
- z ∈ [10.9, 11.8]: solid = disc − af2 hex. The pocket void is af2 hex; the ring annulus (between af2 and af1) is SOLID here.
- So the ring annulus's bottom face (z=10.9, between af2 and af1 hexes): directly below it (z=10.9−ε) is the af1 hex VOID. Unsupported. Its inner edge (af2 hex boundary) continues upward as the af2 wall (ring band inner wall). Its outer edge (af1 hex boundary) — below it is the af1 wall for z<10.9. So the ring annulus outer edge is supported by the af1 wall top rim (line contact).

When printing: layer at z=10.9–11.1 (first ring layer, 0.2 mm): the annulus region. The extrusion for a 0.175 mm wide annulus: one line, centered on the annulus path, ~0.42 mm wide → it will overlap BOTH the af1 wall top (outer) and spill slightly into the af2 void (inner). The outer spill fuses to the wall below (support!), the inner spill hangs over the af2 void by ~0.1 mm. So the ring prints essentially supported on its outer edge with a slight inner overhang. Totally printable. ✓ Same at the ring top: at z=11.8, pocket widens from af2 back to af1 — the pocket wall above the ring is the af1 wall starting at z=11.8, overhanging the ring's... no: above z=11.8, void = af1 hex (wider) — the solid above the ring is disc − af1 hex; the ring top face (z=11.8, between af2 and af1) faces UP into the wider void above? That upward-facing ledge prints fine (it's just a normal top surface... well, it's the TOP of the ring = a horizontal surface facing up, printed as the top layer of the ring, then the walls above rise from the af1 boundary). ✓ No problem.

So printing the pocket-up: only concern was ring underside — resolved: outer edge supported, tiny inner overhang. ✓

What about the mouth loft (45° chamfer at top)? Printing pocket-up: the mouth is at the very top; the chamfer widens upward → overhanging inward?? A 45° wall overhang prints OK (FDM handles 45°). ✓ And I extended the loft 0.5 past the top face so the cut is clean. ✓

3. **Nut seating depth vs ring position:** nut h 4.7, pocket depth 5.1, ring band 1.0–1.9 mm above nut bottom. The nut's corner chamfers at its bottom face extend up ~0.5–0.8 mm (for M5, chamfer ~0.5 mm high × 30°... roughly). The ring band at 1.0–1.9 above nut bottom — just above the chamfer zone. ✓ Good.

4. **Torque transmission:** ring + slip interference (0.05/side in slip zones) → the nut is snug in slip zones too (0.10 over nominal means 0.05/side clearance — that's actually a loose slip fit; the ring provides the real grip). When you crank the knob, torque passes through the ring contact. PLA creep under repeated high torque? The ring is 0.9 mm tall; pressure at flats... For a hand knob this is fine; the coupon verifies.

Hmm, actually let me reconsider one thing: should the snap ring undersize be less aggressive? The user said "presses into the knob by hand". A 0.25 undersize hex — pressing by thumb — I estimated firm but doable. The coupon covers 0.15/0.25/0.35. The middle (0.25) is the shipped value. I stand by it, with the reprint note.

5. **The bolt hole Ø5.5:** bolt shank Ø5.0 → 0.25/side clearance. Threads pass through. ✓ Countersink 7.3 — bolt head isn't in the knob (bolt head is elsewhere; this is a threaded-through knob). ✓

6. **"Bolt goes through the nut and out the other side":** ✓ through-hole Ø5.5 from pocket floor to exit face.

7. **Nut "sits fully inside":** recessed 0.4 mm below the face. ✓

8. **Upside-down test:** ring captures. ✓ Also — hmm, one more failure mode: if the press fit is very tight, pressing the nut in could BULGE the knob or crack the ring? PLA ring wall: the ring band is 0.9 mm tall, the wall around the pocket is thick (knob OD 30, pocket across-corners ~9.35 → ~10 mm of material). Flexing 0.125 mm over a 0.9 mm tall band — fine, elastic. ✓

9. **Print-in-place alternative?** No — user wants hand press-in, no glue. ✓

10. **Does the nut wobble in slip zones (0.05/side)?** After seating, the nut is gripped at the ring; above the ring it has 0.05 clearance. Fine.

11. **Coupon zones identical to knob?** Yes — same ch, s1, ring, depth; only af2 differs. ✓ This is important for the coupon to be representative: press force in a coupon with 44 mm disc vs knob with 10 mm walls — the knob walls are much stiffer?? Hmm! Wait: pressing the nut through the ring requires the RING to flex (expand 0.125 mm/side). The ring is a band in a big solid — the compliance that matters is local: the ring band itself bowing. In the coupon, the material around the pocket: coupon dia 44, pocket corner reach 6.4–4.5 → ~15 mm of material around — comparable stiffness to the knob (~10 mm walls). Close enough for a feel test. ✓

12. **First-layer adhesion / brim:** knobs print fine. Not part of the design submission.

13. **One more check on the loft:** `polygon(6, af1/C)` at z=14 and `polygon(6, (af1+3)/C)` at z=15.5 → slope: af grows from 8.1 to 11.1 over 1.5 mm → 45° in the across-flats direction: radial growth 1.5 over 1.5 z. ✓ 45° chamfer. ✓

14. **Are the hex flats aligned between nut and pocket?** The nut orients itself — hex-in-hex self-aligns at 60° symmetry. ✓

15. **Manual accuracy:** 
- Step: "click ~1 mm short of flush" — nut top sits 0.4 mm below the face. In the coupon, floor 0.9 vs nut 4.7 → nut top at 6−5.1+4.7 = 5.6 from bottom = 0.4 below coupon top face too. ✓ Same.
- "If too tight, reprint with pocket_snap_under=0.15" ✓.

16. **Question phrasing:** fine.

17. **Anything missing from params?** All hardware/world-derived dims are params: nut_af, nut_h (catalog — couldn't measure, noted). knob_od (asked). The rest design. ✓

18. **The `assert s2 > 0.3` in knob code with s2 = 1.0** ✓. Coupon assert: t−depth = 0.9 ≥ 0.8 ✓.

19. **Hardware list:** m5_nut ISO 4032 M5 qty 1. The user's own bolt = external. ✓ Should I include a joint? - fastener: "m5_nut"

2. id: "c_retain_inverted", part hand_knob, feature "snap ring (af nut_af − 0.25)", relation "contains", hardware m5_nut, params [nut_af, pocket_snap_under, snap_ring_h, pocket_slip_zone], check: method coupon, description "coupon pocket-down + tap: nut must not drop"
3. id: "c_blind_floor", part hand_knob, feature "pocket floor (blind, nut_h + 0.4 deep)", relation "supports", hardware m5_nut, params [nut_h, pocket_recess], check: method none, description "solid floor stops the nut 0.4 mm below the face; nothing can push it through the far side"
4. id: "c_bolt_clear", part hand_knob, feature "Ø5.5 centre hole + countersink", relation "clears", params [bolt_hole_d], check: method none, description "M5 shank Ø5.0 and thread crest pass with 0.25 mm/side clearance"

**Hardware:** [{"id": "m5_nut", "ref": "ISO 4032 M5", "qty": 1}]

**Manual:**
1. Print the test coupon (nut_fit_coupon) flat, pocket face up, no supports.
2. Thumb-press the M5 nut into the middle pocket (2 dots) on a hard surface, pressing straight down with a slight twist; it should take firm hand pressure and stop ~0.4 mm below flush.
3. Flip the coupon pocket-down over the table and tap: the nut must stay. Try the 1-dot (0.15) and 3-dot (0.35) pockets for comparison — left easier, right tighter. If 0.25 is too tight for a comfortable thumb press, reprint the knob with pocket_snap_under set to 0.15 (or 0.35 if 0.25 felt loose).
4. Print the knob (hand_knob) as modeled — bolt-exit face on the bed, pocket up, no supports.
5. Press the M5 nut into the knob's pocket exactly like the coupon test: firm thumb press, slight twist, until it clicks past the snap ring and sits ~0.4 mm below the surface.
6. Thread your M5 bolt up through the bottom hole into the captured nut; grip the flutes and turn — the captured nut drives the bolt, which exits the far side. No glue anywhere.
7. Need the nut out later? Lever it over the snap ring with a small flat screwdriver from the mouth side — it's a press fit, not welded in.

Parts refs: step 1 → nut_fit_coupon; 2–3 → nut_fit_coupon + m5_nut; 4 → hand_knob; 5 → hand_knob + m5_nut; 6 → hand_knob + m5_nut; 7 → hand_knob + m5_nut.
